extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and historians of Gothic and Venetian architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for designing and evaluating mouldings, edge decoration, rolls, recesses, tabernacles, and bases in Venetian and northern (Gothic) architecture, with examples and anti-patterns. Emphasises visual effects, material practice (incrustation), proportion, and appropriate ornament choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogtooth ornament usage
rubrics_metrics.description: "The mere dogtooth is an acid moulding, and can only be used in certain mingling with others, to give them piquancy; never alone."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogtooth (pointed leaf or tooth moulding) is a piquant/acidic moulding best employed mixed with other mouldings; it cannot be used alone on principal angles or important fillets without giving an unpleasant, sharp character. Examples: its use in Venetian Renaissance foundations and combination with dentils and other forms; anti-pattern: using dogtooth alone on a main arch fillet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venetian dentil (fillet incision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Venetian dentil' formed by making "the incisions square instead of sharp, and to leave equal intervals of the square edge between them"; described as "the most universal ornament in its own district."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, easily cut ornament that gives force and interest to the edge of arches without diminishing quietness. Widely used due to Venice's incrusted architecture; often gilded/painted (gold on faces and recesses colored alternately). Found in both early Byzantine and later Gothic Venetian work; illustrated by examples in St. Mark's and paintings by Gentile Bellini and Vittor Carpaccio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incrustation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "The whole early architecture of Venice is architecture of incrustation" — buildings of rough brick overlaid with precious foreign marbles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The habit of incrustation determines choice and placement of mouldings (e.g., need for arch armor and fillet treatment). Because faces are veneered, thin marble soffit pieces can project and form fillets suitable for dentil/carved treatment; influences color play and why certain ornaments (Venetian dentil) are ubiquitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fillet enrichment by square incisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrich the fillet "simply to make the incisions square instead of sharp, and to leave equal intervals of the square edge between them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form gives strength and interest to an arch edge while preserving quietness; easy to cut and adaptable to many positions where stone projects. It became the characteristic Venetian dentil and is suitable for gilding/painting. Alternative (anti-pattern): dogtooth alone on a principal fillet is unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge-decoration choice for principal angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid employing dogtooth alone on principal angles because it gives the whole building a peculiar (untempered) look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On a principal angle such as main arches, choose fillet treatments that do not overly 'acid' the composition; prefer square-incision dentils or mingled mouldings. Example: Byzantine architects could not use dogtooth here as it had not been invented; when used, dogtooth must be mingled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roll and recess as complementary devices
rubrics_metrics.description: "The one [roll] is in most cases the negative of the other [recess], and is used to relieve it exactly as shadow relieves light; recess alternating with roll."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should consider rolls (rounded, rod-like mouldings) and recesses together: a recess's depth increases value of surrounding ornament, while rolls provide soft curves and shadow. Use alternation and interruption (rolls interrupting recesses and vice versa) to create rhythm and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roll treatment by subdivision or surface ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their decorative power is, however, too slight for rich work, and they frequently require... subdivision or minor ornament of their own."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small rolls: cut pieces to form Norman billet or Greek bead. Large rolls: avoid notching; cover with flat chasing or inlaid patterns (inlaid/flat chasing blends roll into true shafts). Choose patterns used for general shaft decoration. Anti-pattern: crudely notching a large roll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghost rolls and Flamboyant recess decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Flamboyant ornament formed by "ghosts or anatomies of the old shafts, left in the furrows" — fragments of roll left in recesses worked into tracery and entanglements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deep furrows, leave small fragments of roll/shaft carved hollow to form intricate tracery; this provides intense decorative effect (stone lace-work). Value lies in darkness of recess and complexity of skeletal forms. Beware: such decoration can swallow statues and overpower their purpose (statues can become subordinate/excused).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate physical form vs intellectual purpose of ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep distinct "the consideration of the changes wrought in the mere physical form, and in the intellectual purpose of ornament."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing canopies/tabernacles or other ornaments, distinguish their physical shape and detailing from their symbolic/functional relationship to elements they shelter (e.g., statue). A canopy may be protective, honorary, miniature architecture, or purely decorative; design choices should reflect intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabernacle / niche design and canopy emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'niche' is "a hollow intended for a statue, and crowned by a canopy"; "tabernacle work... reaches its full development when the Flamboyant hollows are cut deepest, and the canopy becomes the more important of the two."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Niche ornament should consider whether canopy or statue is primary; in late northern practice canopies often dominate, and statues become excuses for canopy decoration. Use deep hollows and canopy lacery for rich tabernacle work; but avoid designs where ornament defeats the statue's role unless intentionally prioritised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ball-flower (ball flower) recess decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Recess decoration by ball flower: "leaving a small boss or sphere... at intervals in the hollows... afterwards carved into roses," producing a 'spotted' character to moulding lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable for spotted effect from a distance; rich and delightful when used sparingly. Overuse (applying to every casement or across entire streets) will saturate and weary the eye. Examples: spires of Salisbury and St. Mary's at Oxford as agreeable isolated masses but would be oppressive en masse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base expresses levelness and evenness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main things to be expressed in a base are its levelness and evenness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design base members (courses) so they convey stable, level foundation. Use different colored marbles for distinct horizontal courses to produce marked level bars of color. Protect vertical sculpture by placing in panels to avoid wear; plain panelling often effective. Examples: St. Anastasia (Verona) and Giotto's campanile for color play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of member e (course above slope) for firm beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Member e is "very valuable, as an expression of a firm beginning of the substance of the wall itself"; better to add course e than abruptly begin common masonry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the foundation is stone and upper wall brick, add this member to create a firm transition. Though previously unnoticed in construction chapters, it visually expresses solidity at the base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member d / Xb: emphasise levelness via double rolls and hollow
rubrics_metrics.description: Member d (or Xb) is the essential feature of bases and should have "full expression of levelness and precision"; avoid eye resting on masonry joints by attracting eye to two rolls separated by a deep hollow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the lower part with two bold projecting rolls and a deep cavetto between them so shadows and parallel bars express absolute levelness and conceal joints. This group prevents attention on stone junctions and forms a beautiful connected set of shadow bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spur design and plan-view considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Spurs (props) set against the lower roll are often seen from above; triangular spur's harsh right lines should be replaced by curves of noble abstract character (e.g., salvia leaf curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the spur is visible from above, replace awkward straight lines with elegant curves to strengthen visual effect. The author suggests substituting a salvia-leaf-derived curve into the triangular spur for a superior Gothic base plan (see figs LIX–LX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dentil size and scale by period
rubrics_metrics.description: Earliest dentils are small ("seldom more than an inch or an inch and a half long"); later Gothic dentils "often as much as four or five in length, by one and a half in breadth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale dentils according to period and expressive intent: increase size in late work for bolder effect; choose size relative to viewing distance and overall composition. Plate examples show varying sizes depending on expression of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour and inlay in base members
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct base members in different colored marble to "produce marked level bars of color all along the foundation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mosaic patterns or simple panelling on vertical portions (a, b, c) but avoid excessive richness. When sculpture is used on bases, carve in panels to resist wear. Examples: St. Anastasia (Verona) and Giotto's campanile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-deep cavetto and excessive expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Deeply cut cavetto and excessive expansion of Gothic bases can appear as a "black fissure" or make bases look flat/separated when seen from above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider viewing angles (particularly above) when choosing base profiles: too much expansion and depth of cavetto can produce an impression of separation from the shaft or a fissure between stones and may appear clumsy from certain viewpoints. Balance profile grace with practical viewing concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fillet use in Northern Gothic to produce severity
rubrics_metrics.description: In Northern Gothic the fillet is used "chiefly to give severity or flatness to mouldings supposed to be too much rounded, and is therefore generally plain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fillet can act as a foil for rounded mouldings but is an 'ugly moulding' when overused; in debased Gothic it became a painful feature. Use fillets sparingly and purposefully to control rounding without making the composition harsh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabernacle/niche decoration balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabernacle (niche) decoration is best when recesses are deep and ornamentation does not draw the eye away from the statue unless intentionally designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Niche decoration by leaf mouldings or other motifs can use the recess's gloom to increase value of leafage; but if canopy decoration overwhelms, the statue's role is lost. Design so that ornament supports, not negates, the principal element unless canopy primacy is desired.
